newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close stronger amid firmer currency.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close stronger amid firmer currency.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed stronger on Monday, with spreads to U.S. bonds narrowing, as an appreciating Canadian dollar supported the market in the midst of weaker U.S. Treasuries, analysts said.

"The Canadian market is being supported primarily by the strong dollar I think," said Philip Strathy, vice-president of Strathy Investments Ltd. "(U.S.) housing starts were stronger than expected so that put a damper on the U.S. market."
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.20 at C$103.50 to yield 7.688 percent against the U.S. 30-year benchmark which fell 8/32 to yield 6.93 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds narrowed to 76 basis points from 79 basis points at Friday's close.

Canadian bonds began the session higher, taking direction from U.S. Treasuries, which opened higher helped by swap-related buying and a firm dollar, analysts said. But while U.S. bonds ceded gains after a release of a U.S. report showing a surprise jump in August single family home sales, Canadian bonds remained positive.
"It's been a quiet afternoon. The last signifcant event in market was the 10 a.m. data that took the edge off the bid in the market," said one trader.
"There's more constructive factors behind the Canadian market right now than the U.S.," the trader said.

In Canadian economic news, Statistics Canada reported that the country's real gross domestic product for July rose 0.5 percent after staying unchanged in June. The number was in line with expectations and was largely ignored by the market, dealers said.

There were two major new issues in the Canadian market this moring. National Bank of Canada agreed with a syndicate of underwriters to issue C$150 million of 7.50 percent debentures due October 17, 2011.
Regina, Saskatchewan-based steel producer IPSCO Inc said it agreed to issue C$100 million of 7.8 percent debentures due December 1, 2006.
In other prices, the 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.12 to C$99.08 to yield 7.127 percent. The U.S. 10-year benchmark fell 6/32 to yield 6.70 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds narrowed to 43 basis points from 46 basis points at Friday's close.
The three-month cash bill traded at 3.87 percent against the U.S. three-month bill at 5.04 percent.
